reason: The sources provide strong multi-site support for the discovery of niobium signatures on a white dwarf, indicating a potential second-generation planet born from stellar wreckage.
story: When low-mass stars die, they expand into red giants and shed their outer layers, leaving behind small, dense white dwarf cores. In 1999, the Hubble Space Telescope observed the white dwarf HS 0209+0832 and recorded roughly 100 mystery chemical signatures that astronomers could not identify. Decades later, University of Warwick researcher Jamie Williams reexamined the archival data using an updated chemical database and discovered a surprisingly high abundance of niobium. Niobium and other heavy elements are not produced by normal nuclear fusion in stellar cores; they are synthesized in the death throes of dying stars. Data from NASA's TESS telescope revealed a periodic 4.4-day light variation, suggesting a Jupiter-sized gas giant orbits just 3.7 million miles from the white dwarf. Extreme radiation is stripping the planet's atmosphere and raining niobium back onto the star, proving planets can be born from a star's ashes.
angle: Archival Hubble data solved a 25-year cold case by revealing high amounts of niobium on a white dwarf, offering the first chemical evidence of a second-generation planet born from the ashes of a dead star.

claims.claim: A white dwarf is the dense remnant core left behind after a low-mass star burns through its nuclear fuel and ejects its outer envelope.
A second-generation planet is defined as a world that forms around a stellar remnant from its cast-off material.
Lead author Jamie Williams, a doctoral candidate at the University of Warwick, led the study published in Nature Astronomy.
When the Hubble Space Telescope observed the white dwarf HS 0209+0832 in 1999, it recorded about 100 chemical signatures that could not be identified at the time.
Reanalyzing archival Hubble data with an updated database revealed a high abundance of the element niobium in the HS 0209+0832 system.
The element niobium had never previously been reported or detected in any white dwarf star.
Elements heavier than iron, including niobium, are synthesized during the death throes of stars rather than through stellar core nuclear fusion.
Observations from NASA's retired Far Ultraviolet Spectroscopic Explorer (FUSE) confirmed strong niobium signatures in the system.
NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) observed HS 0209+0832 and detected periodic variations in brightness.
TESS detected a faint brightness signal repeating every 4.4 days around the white dwarf.
The candidate planet orbits the white dwarf star at a distance of about 3.7 million miles or 6 million kilometers.
The candidate second-generation planet is estimated to be a gas giant roughly the size of Jupiter.
Extreme ultraviolet radiation and intense heat from the white dwarf are stripping the outer atmosphere of the nearby candidate planet.
First-generation planets, including Earth and the planets in our solar system, form from material remaining from a star's birth.
Heavy elements rapidly sink into the interior of dense white dwarfs, leaving atmospheres composed almost entirely of hydrogen and helium.
Between 25% and 50% of white dwarfs display atmospheres polluted by planetary or metallic debris.

disputed: Whether the candidate world around HS 0209+0832 is a confirmed planet or an unconfirmed candidate (CNN emphasizes it is currently an unconfirmed candidate, so scripts should refer to it as a candidate planet).
The exact percentage of stars that become white dwarfs (Wikipedia cites over 97% of Milky Way stars, while CNN states more than 95% of all stars).
